## Cost Environments and Electricity Prices

Two `gymnasium` environments share the same battery dynamics and hidden-demand process but
differ in charging-cost model. The stylized environment charges

$$
\operatorname{cost}(t,p)=\alpha_t\exp(p),
$$

with $\alpha_t$ rising from $2.0\times10^{-10}$ to $7.2\times10^{-10}$ across the window; small enough that even 22 kW for all eight intervals stays below the EUR 100 shortage penalty.
This scaling leaves 0, 5, and 11 kW almost indistinguishable while 22 kW forms a separate, far
more expensive tier; the refined grid narrows these jumps and allows more graduated control,
though the cost remains nonlinear. The stylized model is therefore an artificial
power-dependent reward, not a realistic electricity tariff.

The EPEX environment uses ninety daily day-ahead price profiles for the German--Luxembourg
bidding zone (January--March 2025), converted from EUR/MWh to EUR/kWh and linearly
interpolated to the eight quarter-hour decisions between 14:00 and 16:00; day-ahead prices
range from EUR -0.026 to EUR 0.371 per kWh (median EUR 0.110).

Only the day-ahead price -- the current value and the mean of the remaining window, published
one day in advance -- is observed by the price-aware agent. Charging is billed at the realized
price

$$
\pi_t=\pi_t^{DA}+\varepsilon_t,
\qquad \varepsilon_t\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.015^2)\ \text{EUR/kWh},
$$

which is not observable before the decision; $\varepsilon_t$ is a simulated forecast error, not
a second market-price dataset.

Both formulations deviate from a purely quadratic $p^2$ cost: the stylized environment
emphasizes a nonlinear power penalty, while the EPEX environment prices energy procurement
directly. The two are therefore complementary rather than comparable, and a policy learned
under the stylized cost cannot be expected to remain cost-efficient under real per-kWh prices.
